name: Strangers — how many strangers can run code on your laptop
one_liner: Drop your package-lock.json into a web page and Strangers tells you, in one big number, how many separate human beings can push code that runs on your machine tonight — with the named list, the ones who published while you slept, and a shareable card.
problem: Every JS developer runs `npm install` and quietly hands execute-on-my-laptop rights to hundreds of strangers. After a year of Shai-Hulud-style worms (keyv/cacheable Aug 2026, ChainDrop 444 packages, the 19 malicious packages disclosed 2 Nov 2026) developers know it abstractly but have no way to see their own exposure. Today they either run nothing, or run `npm audit` — which only lists known CVEs and says nothing about who can push into their tree — or install a CLI/SaaS (Socket, rsscan, Commit). The result is that the thing Jack Cable's guide tells them to do (cool down deps, shrink the tree, pin and audit) never gets a concrete, personal "here is your number" moment, so nothing changes.
target_customer: JS/TS developers and indie builders who ship with npm/pnpm/bun — the HN, X dev-twitter and r/node crowd. No buyer; free and open source. Secondary: tech leads who will paste the card in a team Slack to argue for cooldowns.
why_now: Supply-chain attacks are the live topic this week: Jack Cable's "highest-impact actions" guide, amplified by Scott Wu, tells everyone to set a 7-day minimum release age and audit dependencies (https://x.com/jackhcable/status/2117731409246978489), and 19 malicious npm packages were disclosed on 2 Nov 2026. The specific data that makes a one-number answer possible is now routinely available unauthenticated from the npm registry: packument `maintainers`, per-version `_npmUser`, the `time` map with per-version publish timestamps, and `dist.attestations` for trusted-publishing provenance (https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md, https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements/). Provenance/trusted publishing only became widespread enough to be a meaningful green/red signal in 2026 (https://getcommit.dev/blog/).
comparables: rsscan --deps (relayshield) does the same counting but as a local CLI with no visual, no card and no watch — it reported 433 packages / 275 distinct publisher accounts in its own example (https://dev.to/relayshield/who-can-publish-into-your-dependencies, https://github.com/relayshield/rsscan). Commit (getcommit.dev) has a free browser audit but it scores individual packages on trust signals rather than producing one personal exposure number (https://getcommit.dev/audit/). Socket is a paid SaaS/CI integration, not a paste-in page (https://socket.dev/features/sca). npmgraph draws the graph but not maintainers or publish recency (https://npmgraph.js.org). deps.dev shows graphs, not people (https://deps.dev/). cooldowns.dev is a config reference page, not a scanner (https://cooldowns.dev/). Dependabot's weekly digest covers security alerts only, not new publishes or maintainer changes (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts). Gap: nobody turns your own lockfile into one shareable human number plus a weekly re-check.
market_note: No revenue intent; it is a free OSS lead magnet. Estimate: the npm ecosystem is tens of millions of developers and lockfile-paste tools (bundlephobia, npmgraph) have sustained traffic for years, so a hit launch plausibly means tens of thousands of scans in week one. Willingness to pay is near zero for the scan itself; the paid version of this space (Socket, Snyk) sells to orgs, not individuals.
risks: 1) Registry rate limits / CORS: a 1,200-package lockfile means ~1,200 packument fetches from the browser; npm can return 429 and CORS has historically been inconsistent on non-200 responses (https://github.com/npm/feedback/discussions/117). Mitigation is concurrency caps, localStorage caching of packuments, and a tiny Cloudflare Worker proxy with an edge cache if needed. 2) The number may feel like doom-scrolling with no action — if it doesn't hand you a concrete fix (the cooldown config line, the 5 worst packages to drop) people screenshot once and never return. 3) Maintainer counting is noisy: distinct emails over-count one human with two addresses and under-count orgs with shared accounts, so a pedant on HN can call the headline number wrong; label the methodology openly on the card.
riskiest_assumptions: Most fragile first: (1) ~1,000 anonymous packument fetches from a single browser session complete without hitting a 429 wall — unverified, needs a 20-minute test before building the rest; (2) developers will paste a lockfile into a web page at all (the "it's all client-side, here's the source" promise has to be loud enough); (3) the weekly re-check is enough reason to return rather than a one-time screenshot.
first_customers: The first 10 come from posting the result of scanning famous repos (Next.js, Vite, create-react-app, the X web bundle) on X and in the HN thread under the next supply-chain incident; then r/node, the Bun and pnpm Discords, and replying to Jack Cable's and Scott Wu's thread with "here's what the 7-day cooldown advice looks like for your actual lockfile".
validation_test: This week: post one screenshot — "I scanned create-next-app: 312 strangers can run code on my laptop, 41 of them published in the last 7 days" — with a waitlist-free link to a static page that only scans three hard-coded famous lockfiles. Pass: 300+ clicks and at least 20 people replying with "do mine" or asking for the repo within 48 hours. Fail: under 50 clicks, and the one-number framing isn't landing.
build_plan: Stack: one static page (TypeScript + Vite, deploy to Vercel/GH Pages), no backend at first; optional 30-line Cloudflare Worker proxy with a 1-hour edge cache if CORS or 429s bite. Data: npm registry packuments at https://registry.npmjs.org/{pkg} (fields: maintainers, versions[v]._npmUser, time[v], dist.attestations, scripts for pre/post-install) and api.npmjs.org/downloads/point for weight. Steps: (1) parse package-lock.json / pnpm-lock.yaml in the browser, dedupe to resolved name@version; (2) fetch packuments with a concurrency cap of ~8, localStorage cache keyed by name@version, graceful partial results; (3) compute the five numbers — distinct publisher identities, packages whose installed version is under 7 days old, packages with install scripts, packages with no provenance attestation, single-maintainer packages above 1M weekly downloads; (4) render the result screen and a canvas-drawn share card (PNG download + copy); (5) a "Watch this lockfile" button that stores a hash of the tree locally and, on return, shows what changed — new publishers, new versions, maintainer changes; (6) a copy-paste cooldown config block (npm/pnpm/bun minimum-release-age) and the 5 worst offenders to drop. Cut for v1: pnpm/yarn/bun lockfile parsers beyond npm's (add after launch), PyPI/cargo, any account, any server-side storage, any "is it malware" verdict.
launch_post:
You run npm install and hand ~300 strangers the right to execute code on your laptop.

Drop your package-lock.json here and see exactly how many, who they are, and which of them shipped a new version while you were asleep.

Runs entirely in your browser. Open source. No upload.
reasoning:
Strangers won because it is the only candidate where one paste produces a number that is simultaneously personal, alarming, defensible and actionable — and where every dependency is a free, unauthenticated public API the builder can call from a static page in TypeScript, which is exactly this person's stack. The taste file prizes one input, one striking output, no signup, open source; this is the security-flavoured roomGPT. It beat Cooldown Check and Provenance Scorecard by absorbing them: each alone is a single stat, together they are a report card with a headline. It beat the HackerTube and follower-growth ideas on freshness-of-data and non-repetition (Canon already mined the HN video dataset; the follower idea needs paid X data). The strongest reason it could fail is that it's a one-time screenshot, which is why sharpening added the watch-and-delta mode and the copy-paste cooldown config — the fix comes with the fear. It does not touch tonight's venture (Outbound serves machine-shop buyers chasing heat-treat vendors; this serves JS developers), and it differs from the library's Regretcheck, which also takes a package.json but answers "what does HN say about this dependency" (opinion mining from comments) rather than "who physically controls what runs on your machine, and what changed this week" (registry identity and timing data). It could grow: the same scan run continuously over an org's repos, with maintainer-change alerts, is roughly what Socket sells — but the weekend version should stay free and personal.

Runner-up (Venture, 7.8): Outbound won because it is the boring step next to a hot category. Two bookmarks pointed at American manufacturing (twentyfour26's autonomous CNC factory) and at agents doing real work; every obvious manufacturing idea — instant quoting, DFM, FAI reports — turned out to be fully occupied by funded players within one screening call. The step nobody had taken was the one where the shop loses control: the parts that leave the building. Research confirmed three things that matter. First, the obligation is real and specific: AS9100 8.4.3 requires the shop to flow the customer's invoked spec, revision and approved-source requirements down to the heat treater or plater, and the failures (wrong revision, missing cert, non-approved source) produce SCARs, shipment holds and scrapped lots — one published supplier term sheet even charges $250 per shipment for missing certs. Second, the gap is confirmed by incumbents' own shape: ProShop, JobBOSS² and Fulcrum record the outside-process PO but there is no evidence any of them chases the processor or matches a returned cert to the invoked requirement; the only such automations found are third-party bolt-ons written for those ERPs, which is people paying to patch a hole. Third, the 2026 agents that do chase suppliers — HappyRobot, Conversight, VoiceRun — are explicitly enterprise; HappyRobot's own material says it is not for small-business self-serve. That leaves 16,300-odd sub-50-employee US machine shops with the obligation, the consequence and no product. GroundControl (YC, ~$3M seed) is the nearest threat and validates the category, but it reviews the incoming customer PO; Outbound owns the outgoing processor PO and the cert that comes back. It differs from the filed Shortfall and Dockproof ideas in buyer and workflow: Shortfall reconciles insurance commissions, Dockproof prevents retail chargebacks pre-ship for CPG brands; Outbound governs a regulated subcontract operation and its document package for a machine shop. Fit for this builder is good — email-in agents, document parsing and approval workflows are exactly UiPath/Maestro-shaped — but this is a 3+ month venture with a trade-show-and-referral sales motion, not an X-native launch, and the builder should go in knowing that. It is 7.8 and not higher because one thing is genuinely unproven: no public data shows a small shop will add a separate line item for this, and I found no benchmark for days lost at outside processors. That single unknown is what the week-one validation test is built to hit.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Outbound — outside-processing control tower for machine shops (flowdown + chase + cert verify). PICK. Named buyer, recurring weekly pain with real financial consequence, confirmed gap in every ERP checked, price band already established by Uptool/1factory.
2. Sipse-style friction-free investing for Indian retail (from @misbahspeaks). Dropped at generation — consumer fintech, heavily regulated, not B2B, no agent edge for this builder.
3. MFD commission reconciliation for Indian mutual fund distributors (adjacent to the Sipse bookmark). Dropped at screen — Mindstack, Creso, REDVision and others already ship AMC payout ingestion and trail reconciliation for MFDs; also near-identical in shape to the filed idea Shortfall (carrier commission reconciliation), so a repeat.
4. Dependency cooldown / minimum-release-age policy enforcement with approvals (from the Jack Cable security bookmark). Dropped at screen — Safeguard.sh already sells configurable package-age policies, gates and exception approval across npm and PyPI; Socket and Aikido are moving in; and it is a developer-tools idea in a crowded market, which this library already has plenty of.
5. Instant-quote / DFM precheck for CNC job shops (from the twentyfour26 bookmark). Dropped at screen — Paperless Parts, Uptool ($195/mo), AMFG, CloudNC Quote Agent all sell AI quoting to exactly this buyer. Closed.
6. FAI / AS9102 report generation for small shops. Dropped at screen — High QA, 1factory, InspectionXpert, DISCUS, GroundControl and CADNexa all occupy it; nothing left for a narrow wedge.
7. Cold-email reputation guardian for AI-SDR users (from the Explee bookmark). Dropped at screen — Instantly, Warmy, Mailforge, Warmforge and Alta all sell deliverability monitoring and domain warming; commodity, and the buyer is a churn-prone solo founder.
8. Cognitive-debt reviewer: flags PRs a human cannot explain, from the Addy Osmani article. Dropped at generation — latent pain, no budget holder, and another developer-tools entry.
9. Plaid-for-benefits wedge: document-reuse layer for a single county benefits office (YC RFS, Gustaf Alströmer). Dropped at screen — a strong signal but a 12-18 month government sales cycle, far outside an evenings-and-weekends builder's reach to first revenue.
10. AI-for-City-Hall wedge: plan-review corrections for small building departments (YC RFS). Dropped — Archistar AI PreCheck already sells city-side AI code and zoning review to 30+ local governments, and the filed idea Backcheck already serves the applicant side of the same correction-letter workflow. Repeat plus a closed gap.
11. Vendor-cert verification for medical-device contract manufacturers. Folded into the pick as an expansion market rather than run as a separate candidate — same workflow, different regulatory vocabulary.

PROJECT
1. Strangers — drop a lockfile, see how many distinct humans can execute code on your machine, plus who published while you slept → PICK. Personal number, instantly postable, weekly reason to return, every data field verified free and unauthenticated. 2. Cooldown Check — paste a lockfile, see which installed versions are younger than 7 days → finalist, folded into Strangers as one panel; alone it's a yes/no answer nobody screenshots. 3. Provenance Scorecard — what share of your deps are published via trusted publishing → finalist, also folded in; too abstract to lead with. 4. HackerTube Shelf — the 6,454 HN videos as a browsable shelf → dropped at screen, repeat of Canon (2026-11-01). 5. Teardown Gallery — a public gallery of Elvar's teardown-skill 3D machine sims → dropped, it's hosting someone else's project, not a tool. 6. Startup Follower Racer — weekly leaderboard of fastest-growing startup X accounts → dropped at screen, needs paid X API and benln's screenshot is already the product. 7. Agent Surrender Score — grade a chat transcript on how much you deferred to the agent (from Osmani) → dropped, judgment is subjective and unfalsifiable, output is a scolding nobody posts. 8. Secrets Sweep — paste a repo URL, find exposed .env keys → dropped at screen, gitleaks/trufflehog own this and scanning other people's repos is sketchy. 9. SIP Friction Meter — visualise how many steps Indian MF onboarding takes → dropped, no data source, narrow audience, and it's marketing for someone else's app. 10. CNC Quote Decoder — upload a CAD part, get a machinability score → dropped, overlaps tonight's venture (machine shops) and needs real geometry processing, far past a weekend.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): summarised twentyfour26 and the state of on-demand CNC bottlenecks (surfaced quoting, setup, outside processes and cert/inspection as the real constraints — this is where the pick came from); summarised Explee (pay-as-you-go AI SDR at ~$0.04/email, crowded field — killed candidate 7 early); summarised the Jack Cable security guide (npm cooldown / minimum release age advice — seeded candidate 4) and the Addy Osmani cognitive-debt article. Screening pot (6 of 6): one search each on CNC quoting software (Paperless Parts, Uptool, AMFG — closed), dependency-cooldown tooling (Safeguard.sh — closed), Indian MFD back-office software (Mindstack, Creso, REDVision — closed and a repeat of Shortfall), outside-process vendor tracking (thin results, the promising signal), cold-email deliverability (Instantly, Warmy — closed), FAI/AS9102 software (High QA, 1factory, GroundControl — closed). Deep research pot (12 of 12): ERP handling of outside processing and user complaints; dedicated outside-processing/subcontract products and ERP pricing; AI voice agents chasing supplier dates (HappyRobot/Conversight/VoiceRun) and whether they serve SMBs; AI-for-City-Hall landscape (Archistar) which killed candidate 10; GroundControl's PO Review category, funding and pricing model; AS9100 8.4.3 flowdown obligations and failure consequences; cert-package assembly effort and the $250-per-shipment penalty example; RFQ/quoting economics for sub-20-person shops; US machine-shop establishment counts and expediter roles; CoC-vs-PO automated checking (LandingAI, Certivo); what actually goes in an outside-process PO packet and how revision errors happen. Deep research reshaped the idea twice: it closed quoting and FAI, and it pushed the wedge from date-chasing to the document loop. Sharpening pot (5 of 5): confirmed SMB software price bands (Uptool $195-495, 1factory $75/user/mo, ProShop ~$500-715) for market_pull; confirmed aerospace/defense backlog growth (PwC, Oliver Wyman) for timing; confirmed no ERP does the chase-and-file loop natively (only third-party bolt-ons) for gap; checked go-to-market channels for small shops (founder-led, trade media, referrals — tempered the wedge score); checked whether an email-in procurement agent already exists as a product (FactoryJet is a custom-build agency, not a packaged product — leaves the gap open). Investor signals weighed: a16z "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li) and "AI reinforces business models" / "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" supported the pick; YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" and "AI for City Hall" were both tested — the first reinforced the pick's framing, the second was dropped after Archistar and the filed Backcheck idea closed it. YC's space, robots-in-America and data-center-supply-chain signals were set aside as capital-intensive and far outside this builder's reach.
Sharpening (7 to 7.8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6.5). The first shape was a generic "outside-processing tracker: see what's out and chase the date." Research showed that half is crowded from both ends: every job-shop ERP already records an outside-process PO, and HappyRobot, Conversight and VoiceRun all now sell supplier delivery-date chasing agents. Change to the idea: moved the centre of gravity from date-chasing to the regulated document loop — flow the customer's invoked spec revision and quality clauses into the processor PO, then verify the returned cert against exactly those requirements, with date-chasing as the supporting feature. Evidence that the reshaped version holds: Perplexity on AS9100 8.4.3 confirmed flowdown to special-process suppliers is mandatory and that wrong-revision or missing-cert failures produce SCARs, shipment rejection and audit findings; a Perplexity sweep of ERPs found no native "email the processor and auto-file the cert against the requirement" loop in ProShop, JobBOSS² or Fulcrum, and the only such capability found was third-party bolt-on automations — i.e. people are building it by hand; LandingAI does PO-vs-CoC checking but sells to electronics enterprises, not job shops. gap 6.5→8, pain 7→8.

Round 2 — weakest criterion: market_pull (6.5). Worry: can a 25-person shop pay for another tool, and who signs? Change to the idea: narrowed the buyer from "any machine shop" to AS9100/defense-exposed shops of 10-80 people where the owner or quality manager signs, and set the price inside an existing budget band rather than inventing one. Evidence: Uptool publishes $195/month with most shops at $195-495; 1factory lists $75/user/month with a 5-user minimum including CoC and SCAR workflows; ProShop is estimated ~$500-715/month for small shops — so $300-600 is a familiar number. PwC's near-15,000-unit commercial backlog and >50% three-year defense backlog growth, plus Oliver Wyman's finding that 45% of suppliers cannot double output within a year, support rising regulated work at exactly these shops. What did NOT survive: I looked for a quantified "days lost at outside processors" or job-shop on-time-delivery benchmark and found none, and no public evidence that shops buy a standalone line item for this specific workflow. So market_pull moved only 6.5→7.5, not higher, and the validation test was written to attack precisely that hole. timing 7.5→8 on the 2026 supplier-chasing agent category plus the a16z multimodal-data signal. wedge held at 7.5: v1 is email-in, no ERP integration, sellable in weeks, but it is a regulated-document product so trust-building slows the first close.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Karpathy HackerTube dataset (confirmed the zip is 6,454 videos + 39,834 labelled comments + a 150-topic taxonomy — but Canon already in the library covers that angle, so I dropped it); the Jack Cable security guide behind the Scott Wu bookmark (the 7-day minimum release age, lockfile and credential advice became the spine of tonight's pick); and the Addy Osmani article (critical thinking when agents do the work — interesting but produced only essay-shaped candidates). Screening pot (5/5): checked cooldown tooling (cooldowns.dev is a config reference, not a scanner), lockfile paste-in prior art (Socket is CI/SaaS, npmgraph draws graphs not people), startup-follower-growth trackers (crowded, and the data needs paid X API), and "too new dependency" checkers (all CLI/CI, no web). Deep pot (8/8): verified registry.npmjs.org packument fields (maintainers, _npmUser, time, dist.attestations, hasInstallScript in lockfiles), CORS and anonymous rate-limit reality, the downloads API, and the closest prior art — rsscan --deps, which proves the counting works (433 packages → 275 publishers) but is a CLI with no visual, no card and no watch. Sharpen pot (4/4, counted within deep/sharpen split): confirmed Dependabot's weekly digest is security-alerts-only, confirmed trusted-publishing adoption is a live 2026 story, confirmed no free web tool produces an aggregate trust-footprint number. Net change: the idea moved from "pretty dependency visual" to "one personal number + weekly delta + copy-paste fix", and buildability was capped at 8 because of the unproven 1,000-fetch rate-limit question.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6 before). The v1 was a one-time number: scan, screenshot, done. Change to the idea: a "Watch this lockfile" mode that stores the tree fingerprint locally and, when you come back (or after a weekly nudge), shows the delta — which of your dependencies published a new version, which gained or changed maintainers, which are still inside the 7-day cooldown window. Research: npm packuments carry per-version publish timestamps in the `time` map and per-version `_npmUser`, so the delta is computable client-side with no backend (https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md); and I checked the obvious incumbent — Dependabot's weekly digest covers security alerts only, not "who published into your tree this week", and nothing found does maintainer-change tracking for individuals (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts). Usefulness 6 → 8. Round 2 — weak criterion: freshness (7 before). Added the provenance/trusted-publishing dimension: show what share of your tree is published through OIDC trusted publishing with an attestation versus a long-lived token. Research confirmed `dist.attestations` is exposed in packuments and trusted publishing only reached meaningful adoption in 2026, with roughly half of npm's top packages still not using it (https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements/, https://getcommit.dev/blog/). That makes the headline genuinely not-computable-cleanly a year ago. Freshness 7 → 8. Buildability held at 8 rather than 9: registry CORS is documented as supported but historically inconsistent on error responses (https://github.com/npm/feedback/discussions/117) and anonymous 429s are real, so a tiny proxy may be needed — checked, but not proven at 1,000-package scale.
prototype_summary: An interactive "Strangers" prototype that scans a sample package-lock.json and reveals how many strangers can run code on your machine, with filterable package tabs, a watch-mode diff panel, cooldown fix config, and a shareable stat card.
